# Related literature {#sec-literature}

The study joins two literatures that are each well populated on their own side and rarely meet: work showing that transformers trained across many dynamical systems match the optimal filter or the Bayes predictor in squared error, and work applying the tests of the expectations literature to machine forecasters. Each strand below closes with the point at which this paper departs from it. The section ends with the search made before the pre-registration was frozen and its limits.

## Overreaction in human and survey expectations

The diagnostics used here come from the study of human expectations. @coibion2015information regress consensus forecast errors on consensus forecast revisions; a positive coefficient means that errors follow revisions, which is underreaction to news, and they read it as evidence of information rigidity. @bordalo2020overreaction run the same regression forecaster by forecaster and find that individual professional forecasters more often overreact, with a negative coefficient, even where the consensus underreacts. @afrouzi2023overreaction move the question to the laboratory, where the process is known: subjects forecast AR(1) series with persistence fixed per subject, and the slope of the forecast on the current value, the implied persistence, exceeds the true persistence by more the less persistent the series is. Their account, developed in the working-paper version under the title "Overreaction and Working Memory" [@afrouzi2020overreaction], ties overreaction to imperfect use of past information.

Two older lines of work bear on the reference point, and they are the reason the benchmark of this paper is not offered as a new idea. The first is learning about parameters. @timmermann1993how and @lewellen2002learning show that an investor who must estimate the parameters of the process produces, with no irrationality, the predictability that full-information tests read as inefficiency, and @farmer2024learning make the same argument for the anomalies of survey and market forecasts. The second is limited memory: @dasilveira2019noisy and @dasilveira2020optimally derive overreaction from a forecaster who recalls the past imperfectly, which is also the account of @afrouzi2023overreaction. The window W of this paper is the crudest version of that constraint, a hard truncation with no choice of what to remember. What those papers establish in models, the present design measures against an exact benchmark in a trained forecaster.

Three things are taken from this literature. The first is the experimental design: an AR(1) process, the grid of persistence values ({{< var design.rho_grid >}}) and scoring over rounds {{< var design.eval_t_first >}} to {{< var design.eval_t_last >}}. The second is the diagnostics: implied persistence and the error-on-revision coefficient in its individual-level form. The third is the human curve itself, which enters only the descriptive overlay of @sec-overlay. The point of departure is the reference forecast. In the experiment and in the survey regressions a forecast is compared with the full-information rational forecast. Here it is compared with a Bayesian who shares the forecaster's prior and information, and a memory length W makes the limited use of past information literal.

## Transformers as optimal filters and Bayes predictors

A separate literature asks whether transformers trained across many instances of a task learn the optimal estimator. @balim2023can train a transformer across many linear systems and find that on unseen systems it matches the Kalman filter's output-prediction error. @akram2024transformers find that in-context predictions match the Kalman filter in linear-Gaussian systems and approach nonlinear filters elsewhere. On the theory side, @vladarean2026learning argue that the optimal single linear-attention layer equals one gradient step on a window-size-one autoregression objective, with larger windows linked to preconditioned conjugate gradient, so that attention fits a fixed-window autoregression rather than recovering the system; @cole2025context give approximation bounds and a depth separation for in-context learning of noisy linear dynamical systems, with a non-vanishing lower bound for single-layer linear transformers; and @sander2024how study in-context learning of noiseless autoregressive processes. @raventos2023pretraining train transformers from scratch on linear regression and find that they behave like the Bayes estimator for the pretraining prior below a threshold of task diversity, and like the estimator for the underlying continuous prior above it. @muller2022transformers train transformers on data sets drawn from a prior so that the network approximates the posterior predictive distribution, which is the logic of @prp-optimal used as a method.

These papers lead one to expect H1. In our setting ρ is drawn afresh from a continuous prior for every training sequence, the high-diversity case of @raventos2023pretraining, and matching the optimal filter in squared error is the headline of @balim2023can and @akram2024transformers. H1 is therefore treated as a near-replication in a scalar AR(1). The departures are three. This literature measures accuracy; it does not ask whether the residual deviations are over- or underreaction. It compares a network with the full-sample optimum; it does not separate an information limit from a learning failure, which is what a benchmark with exactly the network's inputs does. And where it varies context length it does so for expressivity or sample-complexity results, not as a map of bias against an information-matched forecaster. The fixed-window view of @vladarean2026learning describes what attention computes; window-Bayes is its behavioural counterpart, the best any forecaster restricted to that window can do. The depth results of @cole2025context bear on our size axis, where the one-layer model is the one that departs (@sec-exploratory).

The closest design is @acero2026what, who trains GPT-style models from scratch on order flow from a simulator with known latent parameters and finds that the learned predictive matches the exact Bayes optimum in log loss, with the regime decodable from activations. It shares the method, from-scratch training on a known simulator with an exact Bayes reference. It measures next-token log loss and representations, not forecast slopes or revisions; it has no information-matched benchmark and no sweep over context length; and it makes no link to the expectations literature. @chib2025learning train a transformer on panels simulated from a macroeconomic model mixed with real data and compare it with a vector autoregression on accuracy and likelihood, without an exact Bayes reference or bias diagnostics.

## Expectations tests on machine forecasters

The second literature applies expectations tests to machines. @frank2023behavioral show that rational forecasters with optimal regularisation fail forecast-efficiency tests against full information, and find overreaction in machine-learning earnings forecasts at a two-year horizon. Their argument is in the same spirit as ours: a violation of a full-information test need not be irrationality. With real analyst data the true process is unknown, so the reference remains the full-information forecast; our design makes the comparison with a Bayesian holding the same information exact. @gao2026debiasing give pretrained language models series of the kind used by @afrouzi2023overreaction, find that the models extrapolate, and reduce it by fine-tuning on rational forecasts. @bini2026behavioral run a broad battery of human-bias experiments, forecasting tasks among them, on families of language models and find that larger models often answer belief tasks rationally. @chen2024what find that a language model's return forecasts over-extrapolate from recent returns, and @wang2026bridging study the weights language-model agents put on priors and signals in a behavioural Kalman-filter framework. All of these measure pretrained language models, prompted with numbers, against the full-information forecast. None trains a network from scratch on a known process, and none has an exact or information-matched Bayes benchmark.

## What is added, and the search behind that claim

Matching the optimal filter in squared error is established, and H1 adds little to it. What this paper adds is a combination: the slope diagnostics of the expectations literature, measured in excess of an exact Bayes forecaster with the same information, across memory lengths and model sizes, on networks whose training objective is known to have the conditional mean as its optimum, under rules fixed in advance.

A search made on {{< var novelty.date >}}, before the pre-registration was tagged, found no paper that does this, and none that combines any two of its three pieces (the expectations diagnostics; a network trained from scratch on a known process with an exact Bayes reference; an information-matched benchmark swept across context length). The search used OpenAlex title-and-abstract queries, the arXiv interface and web searches, and verified each neighbour by identifier; its queries and hit counts are in the repository (`docs/novelty_check.md`). It has stated blind spots: it could not query OpenReview, Google Scholar or SSRN directly, many SSRN records in OpenAlex carry no abstract, and a preprint posted in the days before the search could have been missed. The works on parameter learning, on limited memory and on networks fitted to prior draws cited above were not found by that search; they were added after it, at review, and none of them combines the three pieces either. The claim of novelty is accordingly a claim about what that search found.
